why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
claim: This type is eight first-order all-pass sections in series, summed with the dry signal rather than averaged with it, running at thirty-two kilohertz. One byte moves every section's corner together, which puts four cancellations in the audible band at fixed ratios read in the tangent of frequency -- so they crowd towards each other in hertz as the byte takes them up, and the top ones leave the band rather than staying four.
named: a phaser as the period built one: an all-pass ladder mixed back with the input
adds: The archive says what the manual byte did to each third-octave band at nine settings. It does not say those profiles are the magnitude of a phase -- that the dips are cancellations between a signal and a delayed-in-phase copy of itself rather than filters with stopbands, that there are eight sections rather than six or ten, that the dry and wet are summed rather than averaged, or that the chain runs at thirty-two kilohertz. Each is a structure fitted to the readings, and the fit is what this holds.
refutedBy: A setting of the manual byte whose profile has a number of cancellations no single section count explains, or notches whose positions in the tangent of frequency are not fixed multiples of one corner. Either would say the sections do not share a corner, which is the whole of this structure. A rate other than thirty-two kilohertz fitting better once the profile can be read above sixteen would refute the rate without touching the section count.

eraPriors.claim: A phaser of this period is a cascade of first-order all-pass sections summed with the input.
eraPriors.why: It is the one structure that gives evenly spaced notches for the cost of two multiplies a section, and a fixed-point part can run eight of them where it could not run eight biquads.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The notches did not sit at the ratios an all-pass ladder fixes, or their count did not match one section count across every setting. Both were measured: four notches at the bottom of the byte, at 3.30 and 2.20 times each other against the 3.36 and 2.24 that eight sections fix.

alternatives.reading: Four second-order all-pass sections rather than eight first-order ones.

separatedBy.observable: Nothing this or any run can read.

predicts.four second order: The same notches, exactly, wherever the pole pairs sit on the real axis -- and notches at other ratios wherever they do not.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: The notch ratios are read to 0.030 octaves, against the 0.089 octaves a pole pair off the real axis would have to move them by before it was a different chain.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: Two second-order all-pass sections with their poles on the real axis are two first-order ones, so at the only setting where this reading reproduces, it is not a second structure -- it is the same chain written in pairs. Anywhere else its phase runs steeper near each corner and the notch ratios move off the ones measured here, which the fit already bounds. So the difference is how somebody implemented it and not what the unit does, and there is no run to queue. This was nearly queued as one: the resonance byte was taken to be the thing that would separate them, and the record beside this one shows it is a feedback path around the ladder, which both readings share.

alternatives.reading: The corner table is a law in the byte rather than the readout published here.

separatedBy.observable: Nothing the unit's output can be asked.

predicts.a readout: The corners at the settings measured, and nothing about the rest.
predicts.a law: The same corners, since a law that returns these numbers and a table holding them differ in where the numbers come from and in nothing that comes out.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: The corner is read to 0.030 octaves at every setting asked, and twenty-two of the hundred and twenty-eight have been asked.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: The run that was queued here has been made. It asked every eighth value and the three pairs that straddle a stride of eight, to find out whether the byte repeats in blocks the way this unit's filter corners do -- which is the one shape that would have told a stored table from a computed one on this machine. It does not: the corner moves at every setting, 0.056 octaves from 7 to 8 against 0.307 from 8 to 15. With no repeats to count, a table of a hundred and twenty-eight entries and a formula return the same hundred and twenty-eight numbers, and the output is the only thing here that can be asked. This is the state the effect level class is already in for the same reason.
